claim: Homing-based gene drives, engineered using CRISPR/Cas9, have been proposed to spread desirable genes throughout populations.
source: Homing-based gene drives, engineered using CRISPR/Cas9, have been proposed to spread desirable genes throughout populations.
evidence: This is a general statement about gene drives supported by the broader scientific literature context provided in the manuscript.

claim: Invasion of homing-based gene drives can be hindered by the accumulation of resistant alleles.
source: However, invasion of such drives can be hindered by the accumulation of resistant alleles.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations throughout the manuscript and is established knowledge in the gene drive field.

claim: The authors engineered a confinable population modification home-and-rescue (HomeR) drive in Drosophila targeting an essential gene.
source: To limit this obstacle, we engineer a confinable population modification home-and-rescue (HomeR) drive in Drosophila targeting an essential gene.
evidence: This is the primary experimental work described in the manuscript with detailed methods and results.

claim: Resistant alleles that disrupt the target gene function in the HomeR system were recessive lethal and therefore disadvantaged.
source: In our experiments, resistant alleles that disrupt the target gene function were recessive lethal and therefore disadvantaged.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that LOF alleles in the essential gene PolG2 result in lethality.

claim: HomeR can achieve an increase in frequency in population cage experiments.
source: We demonstrate that HomeR can achieve an increase in frequency in population cage experiments, but that fitness costs due to the Cas9 insertion limit drive efficacy.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the population cage experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Fitness costs due to the Cas9 insertion limit HomeR drive efficacy.
source: We demonstrate that HomeR can achieve an increase in frequency in population cage experiments, but that fitness costs due to the Cas9 insertion limit drive efficacy.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2C showing decline of Cas9 frequency over generations.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 homing-based gene drives have been laboratory-tested for population modification.
source: These challenges have fostered the development of innovative population control technologies such as Cas9/guideRNA (Cas9/gRNA) homing-based gene drives (HGDs) (Champer et al., 2016; Esvelt et al., 2014) which have been laboratory-tested for either population modification (Adolfi et al., 2020; Carballar-Lejarazú et al., 2020; Gantz et al., 2015; Li et al., 2020; Pham et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 homing-based gene drives have been laboratory-tested for population suppression.
source: or population suppression (Hammond et al., 2016; Kyrou et al., 2018; Simoni et al., 2020) to reduce and eliminate wild disease-transmitting populations of mosquitoes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: HGDs can suffer from the formation of resistant alleles, hindering their efficacy.
source: Despite significant progress, HGDs are still an emerging technology that can suffer from the formation of resistant alleles, hindering their efficacy (Adolfi et al., 2020; Carballar-Lejarazú et al., 2020; Gantz et al., 2015; Hammond et al., 2016; Kandul et al., 2020; Kyrou et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020; Pham et al., 2019; Simoni et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: In CRISPR/Cas9, the Cas9 endonuclease cuts a programmed DNA sequence complementary to a user-defined short guide RNA molecule (gRNA).
source: In CRISPR/Cas9, the Cas9 endonuclease cuts a programmed DNA sequence complementary to a user-defined short guide RNA molecule (gRNA).
evidence: This is established knowledge about how CRISPR/Cas9 functions.

claim: To engineer an HGD, CRISPR components are integrated at the target site in the genome.
source: To engineer an HGD, leveraging creative designs originally proposed by Burt, 2003, CRISPR components are integrated at the target site in the genome.
evidence: This describes the general approach to engineering HGDs, supported by citation to Burt, 2003.

claim: When CRISPR components cut the recipient wildtype allele, it is repaired via homology-directed repair (HDR) in heterozygotes, using the donor allele as a template for DNA repair.
source: These components are configured so that when they cut the recipient wildtype (wt) allele, it is repaired via homology-directed repair (HDR) in heterozygotes, using the donor allele (i.e. allele harboring the HGD) as a template for DNA repair.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of homing gene drives, which is established knowledge.

claim: HDR enables the HGD to home, or copy, itself into the recipient allele.
source: This enables the HGD to home, or copy, itself into the recipient allele (Alphey et al., 2020; Champer et al., 2016; Esvelt et al., 2014) (referred to as homing from hereon).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Many HGDs were developed in several insect species.
source: This general architecture for HGD was quickly adopted, and many HGDs were developed in several insect species (Gantz et al., 2015; Hammond et al., 2016; Kandul et al., 2020; Kyrou et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020; Simoni et al., 2020; Verkuijl et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: HGDs unintentionally promote the formation of resistant alleles through mutagenic repair.
source: However, it soon became widely apparent that HGDs unintentionally promote the formation of resistant alleles through mutagenic repair.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent explanation and citations in the manuscript.

claim: When resistant alleles are positively selected, they can hinder HGD spread in laboratory cage populations.
source: When these alleles are positively selected, they can hinder HGD spread in laboratory cage populations (Champer et al., 2017; Hammond et al., 2017; Kandul et al., 2020; KaramiNejadRanjbar et al., 2018; Oberhofer et al., 2018), with one exception that targeted a conserved sex determination gene for population suppression (Kyrou et al., 2018; Simoni et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: One HGD that targeted a conserved sex determination gene for population suppression was an exception to resistance hindering drive spread.
source: When these alleles are positively selected, they can hinder HGD spread in laboratory cage populations (Champer et al., 2017; Hammond et al., 2017; Kandul et al., 2020; KaramiNejadRanjbar et al., 2018; Oberhofer et al., 2018), with one exception that targeted a conserved sex determination gene for population suppression (Kyrou et al., 2018; Simoni et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kyrou et al., 2018 and Simoni et al., 2020.

claim: Resistance arises from Cas9/gRNA-directed DNA cuts being repaired by alternative DNA end-joining (EJ) repair pathways, including non-homologous (NHEJ) and microhomology-mediated end-joining (MMEJ).
source: This resistance arises from Cas9/gRNA-directed DNA cuts being repaired by alternative DNA end-joining (EJ) repair pathways, including non-homologous (NHEJ) and microhomology-mediated end-joining (MMEJ), which can introduce insertions or deletions (indels) at the target site(s).
evidence: This describes the molecular mechanism of resistance formation, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Many indels produced by EJ repair produce loss-of-function (LOF) alleles, which can be selected against if deleterious to the organism.
source: Many of these indels produce loss-of-function (LOF) alleles, which can be selected against if deleterious to the organism.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the nature of LOF mutations.

claim: Functional in-frame EJ-induced indel alleles can be generated, which are unrecognized by the same Cas9/gRNA complex and become drive resistant alleles.
source: However, functional in-frame EJ-induced indel alleles can also be generated, which are unrecognized by the same Cas9/gRNA complex and become drive resistant alleles.
evidence: This describes a mechanism of resistance that is established in the gene drive literature.

claim: When resistant alleles are induced in germ cells, they are heritable and can hinder spread of HGDs.
source: When resistant alleles are induced in germ cells, they are heritable and can hinder spread of HGDs (Champer et al., 2017; Hammond et al., 2017; Kandul et al., 2020; KaramiNejadRanjbar et al., 2018; Oberhofer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Both induced and naturally existing resistant alleles can pose significant challenges to engineering a stable HGD capable of spreading and persisting long term in a population.
source: Both induced and naturally existing resistant alleles can pose significant challenges to engineering a stable HGD capable of spreading and persisting long term in a population.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of resistance mechanisms and their effects.

claim: CRISPR-based toxin-antidote (TA) drives were described and engineered to overcome the accumulation of drive resistant alleles.
source: To overcome the accumulation of drive resistant alleles, CRISPR-based toxin-antidote (TA) drives, in which embryos are essentially 'poisoned' and only those embryos harboring the TA genetic cassette are rescued, were described (Figure S8 in Kandul et al., 2019) and engineered (Champer et al., 2020a; Oberhofer et al., 2020a, Oberhofer et al., 2020b, Oberhofer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: TA drives utilize a toxin consisting of a non-HGD harboring multiple gRNAs targeting a vital gene, and an 'addictive' antidote that is a re-coded, cleavage-immune version of the targeted gene.
source: Generally these designs utilize a toxin consisting of a non-HGD harboring multiple gRNAs targeting a vital gene, and an 'addictive' antidote that is a re-coded, cleavage-immune version of the targeted gene.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of TA drives based on published literature.

claim: TA-based drives are Mendelianly transmitted and spread by killing progeny that fail to inherit the drive.
source: These TA-based drives are Mendelianly transmitted and spread instead by killing progeny that fail to inherit the drive (e.g. 50% perish from heterozygous mother).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of TA drives based on published literature.

claim: Alternative HDR-based TA designs were described and modeled.
source: Alternative HDR-based TA designs were also described (Champer et al., 2016; Esvelt et al., 2014), modeled (Noble et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: HDR-based TA designs were recently tested in mosquitoes targeting a recessive non-essential eye pigmentation gene.
source: and recently tested in mosquitoes (Adolfi et al., 2020) targeting a recessive non-essential eye pigmentation gene
evidence: This is supported by citation to Adolfi et al., 2020.

claim: HDR-based TA designs were tested in Drosophila melanogaster targeting either haplosufficient genes or a rare haploinsufficient gene, each demonstrating drive capacity.
source: and in Drosophila melanogaster targeting either haplosufficient (i.e. the non-functional allele is recessive as a single functional copy of the target gene is sufficient for normal function) genes (Terradas et al., 2021) or a rare haploinsufficient (i.e. the non-functional allele is dominant as a single functional copy of the target gene is not sufficient for normal function) gene (Champer et al., 2020b), each demonstrating drive capacity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Terradas et al., 2021 and Champer et al., 2020b.

claim: The authors developed a home-and-rescue (HomeR) split-drive targeting an essential, haplosufficient gene in D. melanogaster.
source: Building upon prior work, here we describe the development of a home-and-rescue (HomeR) split-drive (i.e. Cas9 separated from the drive) targeting an essential, haplosufficient gene in D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is the primary experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: The accumulation of EJ-induced resistant alleles can be reduced by designing the HGD to target the 3' coding sequence of an essential gene required for insect viability.
source: We demonstrate that the accumulation of EJ-induced resistant alleles can be reduced by strategically following four design criteria. First, designing the HGD to target the 3' coding sequence of an essential gene required for insect viability.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental results showing reduced accumulation of resistant alleles.

claim: The accumulation of EJ-induced resistant alleles can be reduced by encoding a dominant rescue of the endogenous target gene into HomeR.
source: Second, encoding a dominant rescue of the endogenous target gene into HomeR.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental design and results.

claim: The accumulation of EJ-induced resistant alleles can be reduced by using an exogenous 3' UTR to prevent expected deleterious recombination events between the drive and the endogenous target gene.
source: Third, using an exogenous 3' UTR to prevent expected deleterious recombination events between the drive and the endogenous target gene.
evidence: This is part of the design strategy described in the manuscript.

claim: The accumulation of EJ-induced resistant alleles can be reduced by exploiting lethal biallelic mosaicism (LBM).
source: Fourth, by exploiting a process we previously first described as lethal biallelic mosaicism (LBM) in which maternal carryover of Cas9/gRNA complexes contributes to RNA-guided dominant biallelic disruption of an essential target gene throughout development thereby ensuring recessive non-functional resistant alleles result in dominant deleterious/lethal mutations that can get negatively selected out of a population (Kandul et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kandul et al., 2019 and experimental data.

claim: Individuals that inherit the drive allele express a dominant re-coded rescue and are protected from LBM.
source: Importantly, individuals that inherit the drive allele express a dominant re-coded rescue and are protected from LBM.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental results showing viability of drive carriers.

claim: Efficient cleavage of the target sequence by HomeR and rescue are requisites to achieve nearly ~100% transmission in the presence of Cas9.
source: We demonstrate that efficient cleavage of the target sequence by HomeR and rescue are requisites to achieve nearly ~100% transmission in the presence of Cas9, which is accomplished mostly by homing in trans-heterozygous females.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data in Figure 1D.

claim: Nearly ~100% transmission of HomeR is accomplished mostly by homing in trans-heterozygous females.
source: We demonstrate that efficient cleavage of the target sequence by HomeR and rescue are requisites to achieve nearly ~100% transmission in the presence of Cas9, which is accomplished mostly by homing in trans-heterozygous females.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Multigenerational population drive experiments demonstrate long-term stability and efficient Cas9-dependent drive of HomeR.
source: Further, we perform multigenerational population drive experiments demonstrating long-term stability and efficient Cas9-dependent drive.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Mathematical modeling demonstrates that HomeR can outperform contemporary gene drive systems for population modification over wide ranges of fitness, transmission rates, introduction frequencies, and release regimens.
source: Finally, we conduct comprehensive mathematical modeling to demonstrate that HomeR can outperform contemporary gene drive systems for population modification over wide ranges of fitness, transmission rates, introduction frequencies, and release regimens.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The HomeR system could be adapted to other species.
source: Given the simplistic design, this system could be adapted to other species.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the design features of HomeR.

claim: PolG2 (DNA Polymerase gamma subunit 2, CG33650) is required for the replication and repair of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA).
source: We chose DNA Polymerase gamma subunit 2 (PolG2, DNA polymerase γ 35 kDa, CG33650), required for the replication and repair of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA; Carrodeguas and Bogenhagen, 2000; Carrodeguas et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carrodeguas and Bogenhagen, 2000 and Carrodeguas et al., 2001.

claim: Loss-of-function of PolG2 results in lethality.
source: whose LOF results in lethality (Iyengar et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iyengar et al., 2002.

claim: PolG2 encodes the small subunit of the mtDNA polymerase gamma, acting together with the large subunit 1 (PolG1) for the replication and repair of the mitochondrial genome.
source: PolG2 encodes the small subunit of the mtDNA polymerase gamma, acting together with the large subunit 1 (PolG1, DNA polymerase γ 125 kDa, CG8987) for the replication and repair of the mitochondrial genome (Carrodeguas and Bogenhagen, 2000; Carrodeguas et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carrodeguas and Bogenhagen, 2000 and Carrodeguas et al., 2001.

claim: PolG2 is a short conserved gene with an ~130 amino acids (AA) C-terminal domain sharing ~55% AA identity with the human PolG2.
source: PolG2 is a short conserved gene with an ~130 amino acids (AA) C-terminal domain (cd02426; Lu et al., 2020) sharing ~55% AA identity with the human PolG2 (Lecrenier et al., 1997; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Drosophila PolG2 LOF mutations are known to confer lethality at the early pupal stage.
source: Importantly, Drosophila PolG2 LOF mutations are known to confer lethality at the early pupal stage (Iyengar et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iyengar et al., 2002.

claim: The C-terminal location of the functional domain in PolG2 facilitates minimal re-coding, making PolG2 an optimal target for a HomeR gene drive.
source: The C-terminal location of the functional domain in PolG2 facilitates minimal re-coding, making PolG2 an optimal target for a HomeR gene drive (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural features of PolG2 shown in the figures.

claim: Both gRNA target sequences for PolG2 are completely devoid of any single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) according to DGRP2.
source: According to the D. melanogaster Genetic Reference Panel 2 (DGRP2) that includes natural variation in genome architecture among 205 D. melanogaster lines (Huang et al., 2014; Mackay et al., 2012), both gRNA target sequences are completely devoid of any single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) indicating a high degree of conservation.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of DGRP2 data cited from Huang et al., 2014 and Mackay et al., 2012.

claim: The genetic cross between either gRNA#1PolG2 or gRNA#2PolG2 homozygous males to Act5C-Cas9, Lig4 –/– homozygous females was lethal for all male progeny.
source: We observed that the genetic cross between either gRNA#1PolG2 or gRNA#2PolG2 homozygous males to Act5C-Cas9, Lig4 –/– homozygous females was lethal for all male progeny (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: gRNA#1PolG2 induced lethality in trans-heterozygous females harboring Act5C-Cas9 in the Lig4 +/– genetic background.
source: Notably, gRNA#1PolG2 also induced lethality in trans-heterozygous females harboring Act5C-Cas9 in the Lig4 +/– genetic background, suggesting that gRNA#1PolG2 is likely more potent.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data and leads to an inference about gRNA potency.

claim: Maternal carryover of Cas9 protein from nos-Cas9/+ females was sufficient to ensure lethality of the F1 progeny harboring gRNA#1PolG2.
source: Furthermore, we found that the Cas9 protein deposited by nos-Cas9/+ females without inheritance of the nos-Cas9 transgene, referred to as maternal carryover (Kandul et al., 2019; Lin and Potter, 2016), was sufficient to ensure lethality of the F1 progeny harboring gRNA#1PolG2
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: gRNA#2PolG2 induced lethality only in a fraction of the F1 gRNA#2PolG2/nos-Cas9 trans-heterozygous flies, independent of sex.
source: while gRNA#2PolG2 induced lethality only in a fraction of the F1 gRNA#2PolG2/nos-Cas9 trans-heterozygous flies, independent of sex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Sanger sequencing of trans-heterozygous pupae revealed expected mutations at PolG2 gRNA target sites.
source: Sanger sequencing of trans-heterozygous pupae revealed expected mutations at PolG2 gRNA target sites.
evidence: This is experimental data from sequencing analysis.

claim: The mechanism ensuring lethality results from lethal biallelic mosaicism (LBM), in which maternal carryover/zygotic expression results in mosaic target gene cleavage throughout development leading to wide scale loss of target gene function.
source: As we previously first described, the mechanism ensuring lethality results from a dominant process we coined LBM (Kandul et al., 2019), in which maternal carryover/zygotic expression results in mosaic target gene cleavage throughout development leading to wide scale loss of target gene function which can be detrimental to viability of the organism if essential genes are targeted.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kandul et al., 2019 and experimental observations.

claim: Both tested gRNAs induced cleavage of the PolG2 target sequences, though gRNA#1PolG2 induced greater cleavage than gRNA#2PolG2.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that both tested gRNAs induced cleavage of the PolG2 target sequences, though gRNA#1PolG2 induced greater cleavage than gRNA#2PolG2 as evidenced by complete lethality of females and males with both sources of Cas9.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing differential lethality.

claim: Neither HomeRPolG2 nor HomeR(B)PolG2 include the Cas9 gene and thus are inherently confinable drives.
source: Fitting with the split-drive (i.e. two-locus) design (Champer et al., 2020a; Kandul et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020), neither HomeRPolG2 nor HomeR(B)PolG2 include the Cas9 gene and thus are inherently confinable drives (Akbari et al., 2015; Champer et al., 2016; Esvelt et al., 2014; Marshall and Akbari, 2018).
evidence: This is based on the design of the constructs and supported by citations.

claim: Both HomeR constructs include left and right homology arms (LHA and RHA) matching the sequences surrounding the cut site of the corresponding gRNA to mediate HDR.
source: To mediate HDR, both HomeR constructs include left and right homology arms (LHA and RHA) matching the sequences surrounding the cut site of the corresponding gRNA.
evidence: This describes the design of the constructs.

claim: The LHA includes a carefully re-coded sequence of 22 or 27 AA downstream from the cut site.
source: The LHA includes a carefully re-coded sequence of 22 or 27 AA downstream from the cut site #1 or #2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B)
evidence: This describes the design of the constructs shown in the figure.

claim: A p10 3' UTR was included to support robust expression of the re-coded PolG2 and to prevent gene conversion between the rescue HomeR allele and the endogenous allele.
source: and a p10 3' UTR to support robust expression of the re-coded PolG2 and to prevent gene conversion between the rescue HomeR allele and the endogenous allele, which proved problematic in previous drive design architectures (Champer et al., 2020a; Champer et al., 2020b).
evidence: This describes the design rationale supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A dominant 3xP3-eGFP-SV40 marker gene was included to visually track the presence of HomeR.
source: Additionally, we included a dominant 3xP3-eGFP-SV40 marker gene to visually track the presence of HomeR (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the design of the constructs.

claim: Multiple independent transgenic lines of each PolG2HomeR and PolG2HomeR(B) were generated using both HACK and direct HDR approaches.
source: Using both approaches, multiple independent transgenic lines of each PolG2HomeR and PolG2HomeR(B) were generated.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods and outcomes.

claim: Establishment of pure breeding, viable homozygous stocks of PolG2HomeR/PolG2HomeR and PolG2HomeR(B)/PolG2HomeR(B) demonstrated a functional rescue of wt PolG2 function.
source: Establishment of pure breeding, viable homozygous stocks of PolG2HomeR/PolG2HomeR and PolG2HomeR(B)/PolG2HomeR(B), demonstrated a functional rescue of wt PolG2 function.
evidence: This is experimental data demonstrating rescue function.

claim: The precision of HDR-mediated insertions was confirmed by Sanger sequencing the junction sites.
source: Finally, we Sanger-sequenced the junction sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) and molecularly confirmed the precision of HDR-mediated insertions.
evidence: This is experimental data from sequencing analysis.

claim: PolG2HomeR/+; nos-Cas9/+ trans-heterozygous females crossed to wt males transmitted PolG2HomeR to 99.5 ± 0.6% of progeny.
source: We found that PolG2HomeR/+; nos-Cas9/+ trans-heterozygous females crossed to wt males transmitted PolG2HomeR to 99.5 ± 0.6% of progeny
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: PolG2HomeR(B)/+; nos-Cas9/+ females transmitted the corresponding PolG2HomeR(B) to a significantly lower fraction of F1 progeny (68.7 ± 6.2%) compared to PolG2HomeR.
source: while PolG2HomeR(B)/+; nos-Cas9/+ females transmitted the corresponding PolG2HomeR(B) to a significantly lower fraction of F1 progeny (68.7 ± 6.2%, two-sided Student's t test with equal variances, p<0.0001; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Genetic crosses of either PolG2HomeR/+; nos-Cas9/+ or PolG2HomeR(B)/+; nos-Cas9/+ trans-heterozygous males to wt females did not result in significant biased transmission to F1 progeny.
source: Genetic crosses of either PolG2HomeR/+; nos-Cas9/+ or PolG2HomeR(B)/+; nos-Cas9/+ trans-heterozygous males to wt females did not result in significant biased transmission to F1 progeny (60.7 ± 5.3% vs. 52.9 ± 4.0% or 54.3 ± 4.0% vs. 51.5 ± 1.8%, respectively, two-sided Student's t test with equal variances, p>0.05; Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 4–5).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Maternal carryover of Cas9 protein by nos-Cas9/+ females significantly increased transmission of PolG2HomeR by F1 PolG2HomeR/CyO females to 66.1 ± 0.8% vs. 52.9 ± 4.0%.
source: Maternal carryover of Cas9 protein by nos-Cas9/+ females significantly increased transmission of PolG2HomeR by F1 PolG2HomeR/CyO females, 66.1 ± 0.8% vs. 52.9 ± 4.0% (two-sided Student's t test with equal variances, p<0.001; Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The higher efficiency of gRNA#1PolG2 to guide the Cas9-mediated PolG2 disruption likely contributes to the higher transmission rates of PolG2HomeR.
source: These results suggest that the higher efficiently of gRNA#1PolG2 to guide the Cas9-mediated PolG2 disruption, which results in lethality (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D), likely contributes to the higher transmission rates of PolG2HomeR, and underscores the importance of selecting an efficient gRNA for engineering gene drives.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data comparing the two gRNAs.

claim: Either homing in germ cells or 'destruction' of wt alleles in the progeny via LBM could contribute to biased PolG2HomeR transmission rates.
source: We hypothesized that either homing (indicating allelic conversion) in germ cells (Figure 1A) or 'destruction' of wt alleles in the progeny of trans-heterozygous PolG2HomeR/+; Cas9/+ females via LBM (Figure 1—figure supplement 4; Kandul et al., 2019) could contribute to biased PolG2HomeR transmission rates.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the design and previous work.

claim: LBM contributes to dominant biallelic disruption of the target gene throughout development thereby ensuring recessive non-functional resistant alleles result in dominant deleterious/lethal mutations that can get selected out of a population.
source: LBM contributes to dominant biallelic disruption of the target gene throughout development thereby ensuring recessive non-functional resistant alleles (R2 type) result in dominant deleterious/lethal mutations that can get selected out of a population (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of LBM with reference to a figure.

claim: In TA drives, one half of the F1 progeny did not inherit the TA cassette, were not rescued, and were killed—ensuring survival of only progeny inheriting the drive.
source: In these TA drives, one half of the F1 progeny did not inherit the TA cassette, that is, not rescued, and were killed—ensuring survival of only progeny inheriting the drive resulting in a rapid spread of the genetic cassette throughout laboratory populations.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of TA drives based on published literature.

claim: The hatching rate of F1 eggs generated by PolG2HomeR/PolG2WT; nos-Cas9/+ trans-heterozygous females crossed to wt males was reduced by 5.6% compared to PolG2HomeR/PolG2WT; +/+ heterozygous females.
source: The hatching rate of F1 eggs generated by PolG2HomeR/PolG2WT; nos-Cas9/+ trans-heterozygous females crossed to wt males was reduced by 5.6% as compared to that of PolG2HomeR/PolG2WT; +/+ heterozygous females (88.8 ± 2.4% vs. 94.4 ± 1.2%; two-sided Student's t test with equal variances, p<0.004, Figure 1B)
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The hatching rate of trans-heterozygous females was slightly lower than +/+; nos-Cas9/+ heterozygous females (88.8 ± 2.4% vs. 93.4 ± 3.7%).
source: and slightly lower than +/+; nos-Cas9/+ heterozygous females (88.8 ± 2.4% vs. 93.4 ± 3.7%; two-sided Student's t test with equal variances, p=0.052; Figure 1B, Supplementary file 6), suggesting some degree of embryo killing.
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: No significant difference was observed among egg-to-adult survival rates for four female types crossed to wt males.
source: Furthermore, we observed no significant difference among egg-to-adult survival rates estimated for four female types crossed to wt males: 72.2 ± 9.4% for PolG2HomeR/PolG2WT; nos-Cas9/+ ♀, 72.2 ± 15.2% for PolG2HomeR/+ ♀, 70.0 ± 17.6% for nos-Cas9/+ ♀, and 71.5 ± 7.4% for wt ♀ (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Only a small fraction of PolG2WT alleles transmitted by trans-heterozygous females were 'destroyed' via LBM.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that only a small fraction of PolG2WT alleles transmitted by trans-heterozygous females were 'destroyed' via LBM—meaning mutated and not complemented by the paternal PolG2WT allele, since it was also mutated by Cas9/gRNA maternal carryover (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data on hatching and survival rates.

claim: The HomeR transmission of 99.5% by the PolG2HomeR/PolG2WT; nos-Cas9/+ females could not be explained simply by the 'destruction' of PolG2WT alleles.
source: Therefore, the HomeR transmission of 99.5% by the PolG2HomeR/PolG2WT; nos-Cas9/+ females could not be explained simply by the 'destruction' of PolG2WT alleles, which would result in the lethality of 50% progeny as in cleave and rescue (ClvR; Oberhofer et al., 2020a; Oberhofer et al., 2020b; Oberhofer et al., 2019) and toxin-antidote recessive embryo (TARE; Champer et al., 2020a) drives.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and comparison to other drive systems.

claim: HomeR biases its transmission predominantly by homing (i.e. allelic conversion of PolG2WT into PolG2HomeR) from trans-heterozygous females.

claim: Rcd1r-Cas9 induced super-Mendelian inheritance of PolG2HomeR in both trans-heterozygous males and females.

source: Finally, βTub-Cas9 did not induce changes in transmission of PolG2HomeR by either trans-heterozygous males or females (55.6 ± 5.7% vs. 55.3 ± 5.0% in ♂, p=0.55; and 51.5 ± 2.1% vs. 52.9 ± 4.0% in ♀, p=0.94, two-sided Student's t test with equal variances; Figure 1D, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Drosophila males bias PolG2HomeR transmission, but this bias is substantially lower than the nearly ~100% transmission of PolG2HomeR in females.

claim: Insertion of HomeR into an essential gene could enable spread into a population by biasing transmission while also inhibiting the accumulation of LOF resistant alleles (R2 type) through a combination of slow-acting Mendelian selection and by LBM.
source: We reasoned that insertion of HomeR into an essential gene could enable spread into a population by biasing transmission while also inhibiting the accumulation of LOF resistant alleles (R2 type, PolG2R2) through a combination of slow-acting Mendelian selection and by LBM (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the design rationale.

claim: Functional resistant alleles (R1) that alter the AA sequence of the target can be generated by EJ repair resulting from in-frame indels, or nonsynonymous base substitutions.
source: However, functional resistant alleles (R1) that alter the AA sequence of the target can indeed still be generated (e.g. by EJ repair resulting from in-frame indels, or nonsynonymous base substitutions) and may hinder drive spread.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of DNA repair mechanisms and their potential outcomes.

claim: In-frame non-silent PolG2R1 alleles may still affect the fitness of their carriers, especially since an essential gene is targeted.
source: While these mutations may partially rescue the function of the target gene resulting in viability, it has not escaped our attention that they may still confer detrimental fitness costs to their carriers resulting from incompletely preserving the function of the essential target gene due to the altered AA sequence(s) in a critical domain and may result in negative selection within a population.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the nature of the mutations and the essential function of the gene.

claim: Silent R1 mutations that alter the nucleotide sequence but not the AA sequence would not be predicted to impose fitness costs on homozygous carriers.
source: On the contrary, resistant alleles that alter the nucleotide sequence, but not the AA sequence, can also be generated, and these are referred to here as 'silent R1' or 'silent PolGR1 mutations'. These silent R1 mutations are expected to be especially problematic to drive spread as these would not be predicted to impose fitness costs on homozygous carriers, and therefore they would be expected to spread at the expense of the drive.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of silent mutations.

claim: The generation of both types of R1 functional resistant alleles (non-silent/silent) is a shared problem of all HGDs developed to date.
source: Notwithstanding, the generation of both types of R1 functional resistant alleles (non-silent/silent) is a shared problem of all HGDs developed to date.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the gene drive field.

source: As expected, we determined that each fly indeed harbored at least one PolG2R1 allele that rescued viability.
evidence: This is experimental data from genotyping the sampled flies.

claim: Two distinct non-silent PolG2R1 alleles were identified, with one non-silent PolG2R1 type induced independently in two populations.
source: Two distinct non-silent PolG2R1 alleles were identified, with one non-silent PolG2R1 type induced independently in two populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of GFP-negative flies after generation 3.

claim: From nearly 150,000 sequence reads generated from 60 randomly selected GFP+ flies at generation 10, the two previously sampled functional non-silent PolG2R1 alleles were not identified.
source: From nearly 150,000 sequence reads generated, we did not identify the two previously sampled functional non-silent PolG2R1 alleles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Two novel non-silent PolG2R1 in-frame indel alleles, 18 and 9 bp deletions, were found in populations #2 and #3 at generation 10.
source: Instead, we found two novel non-silent PolG2R1 in-frame indel alleles, 18 and 9 bp deletions, in populations #2 and #3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Eleven LOF PolG2R2 alleles harboring out-of-frame indels ranging from a 1 bp insertion to a 23 bp deletion were found at generation 10.
source: Additionally, we found 11 LOF PolG2R2 alleles harboring out-of-frame indels ranging from a 1 bp insertion to a 23 bp deletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is experimental data from sequencing analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

source: We inferred that at least 9, 5, and 17 resistant alleles persisted for 10 generations and were rescued by the PolG2HomeR allele in 60 sampled flies from populations #1, #2, and #3, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequencing data and allele frequencies.

source: Since a single PolG2HomeR allele rescues the wt function of PolG2 and can mask the opposite allele at the PolG2 locus from slow-acting purifying selection, it is not surprising that LOF resistant alleles can be found persisting in the population.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic design and experimental observations.

source: Nevertheless, the PolG2HomeR allele spread to the carrier frequency of 96.7 ± 4.4% in the presence of nos-Cas9 vs. 56.9 ± 11.6% without the Cas9 transgene in a time span of four generations (p=0.0004, a two-sided Student's t test with equal variance; Supplementary file 9–10).

source: At generation 10, the PolG2HomeR allele was fixed in four out of five drive populations and continued to drift at moderate frequency in three control populations in the absence of Cas9: 99.9 ± 0.3% vs. 60.8 ± 3.8%, respectively (p<0.0001, a two-sided Student's t test with equal variance; Figure 2B, Supplementary file 9–10), underscoring Cas9 dependence for drive.

claim: Functional R1 alleles imposed fitness costs on seven female carriers sampled in drive populations #4 and #5.
source: Interestingly, we found that the GFP– males were fertile, while each tested GFP– female died in 3 days without producing progeny suggesting that the sampled PolG2R1 allele(s) incurred fitness costs to female carriers.
evidence: This is experimental data from fertility assays.

claim: Four non-silent R1 alleles were identified that rescued the 'short-lived' viability of the seven GFP-negative females.
source: Dead females were genotyped and we identified four non-silent R1 alleles that rescued their 'short-lived' viability (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is experimental data from genotyping shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: All in-frame resistant alleles identified in this study resulted in AA changes and are non-silent.
source: In summary, all in-frame resistant alleles identified in this study resulted in AA changes and are non-silent and importantly we did not sample any silent PolG2R1 mutant alleles.
evidence: This is a summary of the sequencing data from the study.

source: and a frequency of accurate HDR, given cleavage, in females and males of 99.5% (95% CrI 97.8–100%) and 9.6% (95% CrI 8.0–10.0%), respectively.
evidence: This is from mathematical modeling fitted to experimental data.

source: The fitted parameter estimates are consistent with parameters estimated from individual pair crossings (Figure 1D).

source: Notably, we also observed that the frequency of nos-Cas9 decreased each generation down to 4.1 ± 0.2% or 9.9 ± 1.6% in two population types by generation 6 (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 11).

source: These results suggest that the nos-Cas9 incurred fitness costs on its carrier and was therefore negatively selected out from the population.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing decline of Cas9 frequency.

source: We therefore use mathematical modeling to explore multi-release scenarios (below).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach used in the study.

source: When one-locus gene drive (GD) systems are compared for ideal parameter values, HomeR outperforms all other GDs in terms of speed of spread, and reaches near fixation in terms of carrier frequency, as do ClvR and TARE (Figure 3A).

source: HGD displays a similar speed of spread to HomeR initially; however, fitness costs from the targeted gene disruption and LOF (R2) alleles slow the introgression and allow functional resistance alleles (R1) to build up over time, preventing fixation.
evidence: This is from mathematical modeling results.

claim: The HomeR design overcomes fitness reduction and R2 allele build-up by rescuing the wt function of a targeted essential gene.
source: The HomeR design overcomes this fitness reduction and R2 allele build-up by rescuing the wt function of a targeted essential gene (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the design and modeling results.

source: ClvR and TARE perform similarly to each other for ideal parameter values, but reach near carrier fixation ~4 generations after HomeR does for ideal parameter values (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is from mathematical modeling results shown in Figure 3A.

source: When experimental parameters are used for HomeR (HomeR-Exp, in Figure 3A), it reaches near carrier fixation a generation after ClvR; almost on-par with ideal ClvR and TARE systems and significantly better than HGD.

claim: HomeR reaches near carrier fixation for the widest range of fitness and transmission rate parameter values.
source: HomeR also reaches near carrier fixation for the widest range of fitness and transmission rate parameter values (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is from mathematical modeling results shown in Figure 3B.

source: As an HGD, HomeR drives to high carrier frequencies provided its inheritance bias (or transmission rate) exceeds its associated fitness cost.

source: In contrast, drive efficacy of ClvR and TARE is strongly dependent on fitness cost and weakly dependent on transmission rate.

source: Indeed, ClvR and TARE can each only tolerate fitness costs less than ~20% (Figure 3B).

source: This is a consequence of their design, employing a TA scheme, which induces a significant fecundity reduction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B) in addition to other fitness costs.

source: A one-locus HGD also exhibits efficacy across a wide range of parameter combinations, but its efficacy is reduced compared to HomeR due to the build-up of R2 and R1 alleles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D), which can potentially block spread of the HGD in large populations (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is from mathematical modeling results.

source: In two-locus simulations, Cas9 is separated from drive in all designs and undergoes independent assortment during gametogenesis.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach for two-locus systems.

source: The effects of this design change are evident (Figure 3C). Under the same experimental conditions as one-locus simulations, there is significantly more variation in behavior of two-locus GDs, with a reduced speed of introgression into the population and slightly reduced overall efficacy.

claim: HomeR with ideal parameters is more capable than comparable drives in two-locus configurations, though current experimental realizations require improvement.
source: Nevertheless, general trends remain the same; HomeR with ideal parameters is more capable than comparable drives, though current experimental realizations require improvement.
evidence: This is from mathematical modeling results.

evidence: This is from mathematical modeling results and supported by citation.

evidence: This is from mathematical modeling results and supported by citation.

source: This is consistent with fitness costs applied to the Cas9 locus, which is now separated from the effector gene and gRNAs.

claim: The HomeR system mitigates some issues related to drive resistance for population modification.
source: We have engineered a system we term HomeR, for population modification that mitigates some issues related to drive resistance.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental and modeling results.

claim: Multigenerational population drive experiments indicate that PolG2HomeR can spread and persist efficiently in the presence of Cas9, and this persistence is not impacted by induced resistant alleles, including functional resistant alleles (non-silent R1).
source: Multigenerational population drive experiments indicate that PolG2HomeR can spread and persist efficiently in the presence of Cas9, and this persistence is not impacted by induced resistant alleles, including functional resistant alleles (non-silent R1), mitigating a major challenge for population modification HGDs that are not designed to target essential genes.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from population cage experiments.

claim: The re-coded rescue strategy used to develop HomeR was also used in previous Drosophila TA non-HGDs and recent HGDs in both Drosophila and Anopheles stephensi, though each of these examples suffered from potential drawbacks.
source: The re-coded rescue strategy that we used to develop HomeR was also used in previous Drosophila TA non-HGDs (Champer et al., 2020a; Oberhofer et al., 2020a, Oberhofer et al., 2020b, Oberhofer et al., 2019; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B) and recent HGDs in both Drosophila (Champer et al., 2020b) and Anopheles stephensi (Adolfi et al., 2020), though each of these examples suffered from potential drawbacks.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

source: For example, both the haplolethal HGD (Champer et al., 2020b) and the TARE design (Champer et al., 2020a) share similar problematic design architectures that can be unstable as they are susceptible to functional resistant alleles induced via recombination between the promoter including sequences 5' of the coding sequence and 3' UTR regions, which are identical between the re-coded sequence and the wt sequence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C in Champer et al., 2020a and Figure 2 in Champer et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work and figures from those papers.

claim: A haplolethal HGD that biases transmission in females requires a strict germline-specific promoter that limits maternal carryover, otherwise LBM may result in dominant negative fitness costs to its carrier and impede drive spread.
source: Moreover, a haplolethal HGD (Champer et al., 2020b) that biases transmission in females requires a strict germline-specific promoter that limits maternal carryover, otherwise LBM, either mono- or biallelic, may result in dominant negative fitness costs to its carrier (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) and impede drive spread.
evidence: This is an inference based on the design features and supported by citation.

claim: Efforts to find germline-specific promoters in Drosophila proved exceedingly difficult—with previously tested 'germline-specific' promoters such as nanos and vasa showing significant somatic activity at multiple insertion sites.
source: In fact, our efforts to find such promoters in Drosophila proved exceedingly difficult—with previously tested 'germline-specific' promoters such as nanos and vasa showing significant somatic activity at multiple insertion sites (Kandul et al., 2020; Kandul et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: The recent HGD in A. stephensi was designed to target and rescue a non-essential gene for viability (the eye pigmentation kynurenine hydroxylase gene), whose disruption was pleiotropic and only partially costly to female fecundity and survival.
source: The recent HGD in A. stephensi (Adolfi et al., 2020) was designed to target and rescue a non-essential gene for viability (i.e. the eye pigmentation kynurenine hydroxylase gene), whose disruption was pleiotropic and only partially costly to female fecundity and survival (Adolfi et al., 2020; Gantz et al., 2015; Pham et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

source: Notwithstanding, this drive spread efficiently in small, multigenerational laboratory population cages under several release thresholds; however, many drives did not reach, nor maintain, complete fixation presumably due to the viability and partial fertility of drive generated homozygous LOF resistant alleles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), underscoring the critical importance of targeting a recessive essential gene for such drives especially for larger releases.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Adolfi et al., 2020 and inference about the mechanism.

claim: The ClvR system is quite stable, however, it can be cumbersome to engineer—requiring re-coding of the essential rescue gene, including all target sequences within the coding sequence (lacking introns), and uses an exogenous promoter and 3' UTR.
source: Comparatively, the ClvR system is quite stable, however, it can be cumbersome to engineer—requiring re-coding of the essential rescue gene, including all target sequences within the coding sequence (lacking introns), and uses an exogenous promoter and 3' UTR, necessitating precise titration of expression from a distal genomic location with exogenous sequences to guarantee rescue without imposing deleterious fitness costs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the design features of ClvR.

claim: The design features of ClvR may be difficult to accomplish for essential genes requiring complex regulatory elements and networks not directly adjacent to the target gene.
source: These features may be difficult to accomplish for essential genes requiring complex regulatory elements and networks not directly adjacent to the target gene.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential challenges.

source: In contrast to the aforementioned drives, (i) HomeR relies on the endogenous promoter sequence of the target gene to facilitate rescue expression which significantly simplifies the design and ensures endogenous expression of the rescue using native regulatory machinery

source: and (iv) exploits LBM (Kandul et al., 2019) by targeting an essential gene to ensure recessive non-functional resistant alleles result in dominant deleterious/lethal mutations that are actively selected out of a population (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), four important design features that distinguish HomeR from other population modification drives.

claim: The findings are congruent with previous studies demonstrating reduced homing in Drosophila males.
source: Our findings are congruent with previous studies demonstrating reduced homing in Drosophila males (Chan et al., 2013; Chan et al., 2011; Windbichler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Multiple Cas9 lines supporting Cas9 expression in early and/or late germ cells with different levels of specificity were tested and did not achieve high levels of homing as reported in Anopheline mosquito males.
source: We tested multiple Cas9 lines supporting Cas9 expression in early and/or late germ cells with different levels of specificity and have not achieved high levels of homing as reported in Anopheline mosquito males (Gantz et al., 2015; Kyrou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is experimental data compared to published work in mosquitoes.

claim: Achiasmatic meiosis in Drosophila males likely correlates with the weak activity of the HDR pathway.
source: Achiasmatic meiosis in Drosophila males likely correlates with the weak activity of the HDR pathway (Preston et al., 2006), which in turn results in inefficient homing in Drosophila males.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biology of Drosophila and supported by citation.

claim: Mosquito males have chiasmatic meiosis and recombination, which require active HDR machinery in primary spermatocytes, possibly contributing to efficient homing.
source: Mosquito males have chiasmatic meiosis and recombination (Kitzmiller, 1976) that require active HDR machinery in primary spermatocytes, possibly contributing to efficient homing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biology of mosquitoes and supported by citation.

claim: Reduced homing efficacy in Drosophila males should be accounted for when designing HGDs in other species exhibiting achiasmatic meiosis, such as Drosophila suzukii.
source: Reduced homing efficacy in Drosophila males should be accounted for when designing HGDs in other species exhibiting achiasmatic meiosis, such as Drosophila suzukii, an invasive fruit pest.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Results from independent multigenerational population cage experiments indicate that HomeR spreads and persists efficiently in the nos-Cas9 genetic background.
source: Results from independent multigenerational population cage experiments indicate that HomeR spreads and persists efficiently in the nos-Cas9 genetic background (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A single copy of the HomeR inserted at an essential gene provides sufficient rescue and complements the corresponding LOF allele.
source: As expected, a single copy of the HomeR inserted at an essential gene provides sufficient rescue and complements the corresponding LOF allele.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the viability of heterozygous flies.

claim: The PolG2HomeR allele persisted for 10 generations in control cage populations without Cas9 and its frequency drifted >50%, underscoring the lack of major fitness costs to PolG2HomeR.
source: The PolG2HomeR allele persisted for 10 generations in control cage populations without Cas9 and its frequency drifted >50%, underscoring the lack of major fitness costs to PolG2HomeR.
evidence: This is experimental data from the control populations.

claim: The slow-acting elimination of LOF alleles takes especially long time by HGDs targeting non-essential genes or genes whose disruption does not cause complete lethality or sterility of homozygous carriers.
source: The slow-acting elimination of LOF alleles takes especially long time by HGDs targeting non-essential genes or genes whose disruption does not cause complete lethality or sterility of homozygous carriers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; Adolfi et al., 2020; Gantz et al., 2015) underscoring the importance of targeting essential genes.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to published work.

claim: Functional resistant (R1) alleles are a problematic feature shared universally by many kinds of gene drives.
source: Functional resistant (R1) alleles are a problematic feature shared universally by many kinds of gene drives.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the gene drive field.

claim: Functional resistant alleles can still be induced even when an essential gene required for insect viability is targeted.
source: These alleles can still be induced even when an essential gene required for insect viability is targeted (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: No silent R1 mutations (i.e. mutations that change the DNA sequence but not the protein AA sequence) were identified in this study.
source: However, it should be noted that here we did not identify any silent R1 mutations (i.e. mutations that change the DNA sequence but not the protein AA sequence) which would be expected to be fitness neutral.
evidence: This is a summary of the sequencing data from the study.

claim: Each identified in-frame non-silent PolG2R1 allele changed at least one AA and thus may still affect the fitness of its carrier.
source: Each identified in-frame non-silent PolG2R1 allele we found changed at least one AA and thus may still affect the fitness of its carrier, especially since we are targeting an essential gene, preventing such alleles from accumulating at the expense of the drive.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequencing data and the nature of the target gene.

claim: Functional R1 alleles imposed fitness costs on female carriers, which likely limits their accumulation and results in negative selection out of the population.
source: Indeed, we observed that functional R1 alleles imposed fitness costs on seven female carriers sampled in drive populations #4 and #5. This fitness cost likely limits their accumulation and results in negative selection out of the population, in favor of the PolG2HomeR alleles, over multiple generations (Figure 2A–B) again underscoring the importance of targeting an essential gene.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced fertility of R1 carriers.

claim: Multiplexing by encoding additional gRNAs into HomeR may further diminish the probability of inducing functional resistant alleles and further increase drive stability, spread, and persistence.
source: Nevertheless, multiplexing by encoding additional gRNAs into HomeR may further diminish the probability of inducing functional resistant alleles and further increase drive stability, spread, and persistence (Champer et al., 2018; KaramiNejadRanjbar et al., 2018; Marshall et al., 2017; Oberhofer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to published work.

claim: Splitting HomeR into two genetic loci (HomeR and Cas9) integrated on different chromosomes serves as an important molecular containment mechanism.
source: Splitting HomeR into two genetic loci (HomeR and Cas9) integrated on different chromosomes serves as an important molecular containment mechanism (Akbari et al., 2015; Long et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work on containment strategies.

claim: The HomeR element is able to home into wt alleles and bias its transmission, but the Cas9 element, which is inherited Mendelianly, is required for its homing.
source: The HomeR element is able to home into wt alleles and bias its transmission. However, the Cas9 element, which is inherited Mendelianly, is required for its homing.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the split-drive design.

claim: The independent assortment of Cas9 and HomeR limits the spread of HomeR and acts as a genetic 'brake' for the invasion of HomeR.
source: Therefore, the independent assortment of Cas9 and HomeR limits the spread of HomeR and acts as a genetic 'brake' for the invasion of HomeR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetics of the split-drive design.

claim: The spread dynamic of split-HGDs resembles that of high-threshold drives and thus requires a high introduction rate for HomeR to spread into a local population and prevents its spread into neighboring populations.
source: The spread dynamic of split-HGDs resembles that of high-threshold drives and thus requires a high introduction rate for HomeR to spread into a local population and prevents its spread into neighboring populations, which is an important feature for confining drive spread and may be necessary for initial field testing of gene drives (Adelman et al., 2017; Akbari et al., 2015; Friedman et al., 2020; Kandul et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Raban and Akbari, 2017; Raban et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to published work on drive confinement.

claim: HomeR can be further confined by fitness costs to either the HomeR drive itself or to the Cas9 element.
source: Moreover, HomeR can be further confined by fitness costs to either the HomeR drive itself or to the Cas9 element, and our experiments revealed that the Cas9 element imposed significant fitness costs that can impede drive invasion (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Even with significant fitness costs, multiple releases of the HomeR could still enable drive spread and long-term persistence as evidenced by mathematical models.
source: Notwithstanding, even with significant fitness costs, multiple releases of the HomeR could still enable drive spread and long-term persistence as evidenced by mathematical models (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: If unintended consequences arise, HomeR's spread can be reversed by reintroduction of insects harboring wt alleles of the gene targeted.
source: As an additional safety measure, if unintended consequences arise, HomeR's spread can be reversed by reintroduction of insects harboring wt alleles of the gene targeted.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a potential reversal strategy.

claim: HomeR could facilely be converted into a non-localized gene drive by incorporating the Cas9 into the HomeR drive cassette.
source: Notwithstanding, if desired, HomeR could facilely be converted into a non-localized gene drive by incorporating the Cas9 into the HomeR drive cassette and our modeling illustrates that it could perform quite well under this configuration (Figure 3A,B, Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by modeling results.

claim: The split-drive design of HomeR is a safe localized gene drive technology that could be widely adopted and implemented for local population control.
source: Taken together, the split-drive design of HomeR is a safe localized gene drive technology that could be widely adopted and implemented for local population control, and if a non-localized drive is desired for more wide scale spread, HomeR could be adapted for that purpose too.
evidence: This is a summary statement with speculative elements about future applications.

claim: HomeR combines promising aspects of current population modification drives—confinablity, high transmission of HGDs, and resilience to EJ generated resistant alleles similar to TA drives.
source: In sum, HomeR combines promising aspects of current population modification drives—confinablity, high transmission of HGDs, and resilience to EJ generated resistant alleles (R2 type and R1 type that induces a fitness cost) similar to TA drives (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental and modeling results.

claim: Modeling illustrates success of both design aspects of HomeR in linked or split-drive form, demonstrating robust behavior over a range of parameter combinations.
source: Modeling illustrates success of both design aspects in linked or split-drive form, demonstrating robust behavior over a range of parameter combinations (Figures 3–4).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: HomeR's stability and resilience to EJ alleles overcomes a significant hurdle for current HGD designs.
source: This underscores its stability and resilience to EJ alleles, overcoming a significant hurdle for current HGD designs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental and modeling results.
